To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

patients with spinal cord injury who experience neuropathic pain show structural brain changes that differ from those who do not have pain, and that the presence and intensity of pain are associated with these structural changes.
The structural brain changes associated with neuropathic pain in spinal cord injury are related to the degree and presence of pain and involve but extend beyond the sensorimotor cortex."

(1) the presence of pain after spinal cord injury was associated with reduced grey matter volume in primary sensory cortices, (2) this reduction correlated with pain severity and (3) the presence and severity of pain after SCI were associated with structural changes in corticospinals tracts and in the visual cortex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neuroplastic changes that occur after a traumatic spinal cord injury and how they may contribute to the development of neuropathic pain.
the brain mechanisms that underlie chronic pain in spinal cord injury (SCI) patients.
the neuroplastic changes that underlie the development of neuropathic pain after spinal cord injury and how these can be prevented.

the brains of patients with chronic neuropathic pain are different from those of patients without pain.
